summary: We have developed an interactive game targeted towards university students interested in aerospace engineering. Currently, there are problems with traditional assumptions of how weight is the sole primary factor when deciding cost (when there is, in reality, a combination of many factors like altitude, time, types of aircrafts..etc). Additionally, because of the lack of experience in real industry fields, students tend to separate a space mission into multiple components like spacecraft and ground control, rather than understanding how they all interconnect. So, our solution was to focus on the costs when building space missions, since costs are the ultimate constraint when building space missions; yet, something not frequently talked about. Because there are real data that mentions how the current ways of space mission design frequently exceed final costs estimates with an average of over 45% in US Space Systems, our app hopes to lower the gap to prevent future financial skepticism and ensure reliability from the government and its people. In the future, we hope to expand our audience so that space enthusiasts no matter the age can understand the difficulties of building a space mission while balancing trade-offs within a single simulation, and how there are so many factors one have to consider with just the cost alone.
details:
Our project is an interactive educational game that allows students, especially university students studying aerospace engineering or those who want to go into the aerospace engineering field, to experience the process of designing and planning a space mission. Traditional education on space missions often teaches students the individual components, such as the aircraft, ground control, etc. However, they rarely get to experience the process of designing a space mission as a whole. Our project fills in this gap by allowing players to build their own space mission through a budget-based simulation. First, the players select a type of mission they want to design and get the mission objective. Then, they start designing the mission through 4 different segments: launch, space, ground, and user segments. In each component, the players will have to make choices about what they want to implement in the mission, such as the type of aircraft and what kind of communication system they will have with the ground. After the player has finished all 4 segments, the game will run a simulation on how successful the mission will be and will give out a score as well as feedback on their mission. The system will evaluate the players' choices and help them understand the consequences of their decisions. On the final page, the players will be able to see past NASA missions relevant to the type of mission they selected in the beginning (e.g., Selected: Explore another world → Mars Perseverance rover). They will get a brief description of the mission, the budget they used, the rocket they used, etc. There will also be a few links that lead to the official NASA website about the mission. 

The thing that makes our project creative is that we focused on the budget, which is something not many focus on. Notably, there are only a few games/competitions where university students can learn how to balance technical design with real financial constraints (with the very few being the ESA/CNES Cost Engineering Challenge). Additionally, our project makes the complex process of mission design more accessible and engaging, even for people without any technical backgrounds. Rather than reading from a textbook, they can simulate and test multiple missions over and over again, developing a deep understanding of designing a space mission. 

For our development, we used Codex and ChatGPT. ChatGPT helped us brainstorm ideas as well as refine prompts to input into Codex. We mainly used Codex for creating the game, and it helped us improve the game by generating and modifying the code. Our game was built using React, TypeScript, HTML, JavaScript, and CSS.
